newsitem.title: USA: ICI says bond fund investors steady in downturns.
newsitem.headline: ICI says bond fund investors steady in downturns.

text.p: Investors in the $657.8 billion bond mutual fund market are a sturdy bunch that resist shedding shares during market downturns, the Investment Company Institute said in a new study released Wednesday.

"Although they react to market developments, bond fund shareholders do not panic and they do not redeem shares en masse even when interest rates rise sharply," Brian Reid, senior economist at ICI, said in an 11-page report that tracks growth of the bond mutual fund market over the last 20 years.
Reid, who outlined his findings in a telephone briefing with reporters, said that besides being stalwart, investors in municipal, Ginnie Mae, global and other bond mutual funds, are independent.
They tend to buy shares on their own, rather than through company 401(k) plans and individual retirement accounts, Reid said.
He explained that 76 percent of bond mutual fund assets, roughly $446.3 billion of the $587.2 billion outstanding at end of 1995, were owned by individuals.
But of those household holdings, only 20 percent were invested through employer sponsored retirement plans, he said.
By contrast, while individuals hold over two-thirds of stock funds assets, they hold through company sponsored retirement accounts, he said.
Reid, a former Federal Reserve Board economist, said he reached his conclusions after studying bond fund investor behavior during five bond market "contactions" since 1975.

He said the largest one-month selloff by investors of bond fund holdings was when the stock market crashed in October 1987. Total "outflows" from bond funds totaled about 3.3 percent of total fund assets, a drop he called "modest." The smallest was 1.10 percent in October 1979, Reid said.

Reid said investment in bond funds has not been heavy in recent years because of "flat" interest rates. But that is the results of "cyclical" developments in the U.S. economy, and not harbinger of future investment, he said.
"Should interest rates fall and a wider gap open up between long-term and short-term rates, inflows could strengthen, as they did in the mid-1980s and early 1990s," he said.
In other findings, Reid said bond fund shareholders, particularly those holding municipal bond funds, tend to be a bit older, richer, and better educated than stock fund holders.
The "median" stock fund shareholder is 44 and has a household income of $60,000 a year, Reid said. Also, only 18 percent of such investors are retired and 58 percent have completed college.
By contrast, the average municipal bond fund shareholder, for instance, is 50 and has a household income of $60,000. Also, 30 percent are retired and 69 percent completed college, Reid said.

Reid said the number of bond mutual funds has mushroomed since 1940 when U.S. lawmakers enacted legislation that encouraged fund investment. There were only six bond mutual funds in 1940, compared to 211 in January 1984 and 2,170 in December 1996, he said.
The Investment Company Institute is the trade group that represents the mutual fund industry.
